title: [MPS] Process crashes (SIGSEGV/SIGABRT inside Metal) when two Python threads run tensor ops concurrently
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug Running MPS tensor ops from two Python threads at the same time kills the process; there is no Python exception. The same ops on one thread never crash. Reproducer (only `torch`, no model; this is the `threads_arange` case of the attached `repro.py`): ```python import threading, torch DTYPES = [torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16] def worker(iters=60): for i in range(iters): dt = DTYPES[i % len(DTYPES)] a = torch.arange(0, 4096 + i, 1, device="mps", dtype=dt) b = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 2048 + i, device="mps", dtype=dt) float(a.float().sum() + b.float().sum()) ts = [threading.Thread(target=worker) for _ in range(2)] for t in ts: t.start() for t in ts: t.join() print("no crash") ``` Runs on Apple M3 Pro, macOS 26.5.1: | torch | threads | iters per thread | runs crashed / total | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 2.14.0 (PyPI wheel) | 2 | 60 | 3 / 3 | | 2.14.0 | 2 | 5 | 5 / 5 | | 2.14.0 | 1, same ops and total work | 5 | 0 / 3 | | 2.15.0.dev20260919 | 2 | 5 | 2 / 2 | | 2.15.0.dev20260919 | 1 | 5 | 0 / 1 | The process ends with exit 134 and one of these on stderr: ``` -[AGXG15XFamilyCommandBuffer blitCommandEncoderCommon:]:836: failed assertion `A command encoder is already encoding to this command buffer' ``` ``` failed assertion `_status < MTLCommandBufferStatusCommitted' at line 323 in -[IOGPUMetalCommandBuffer setCurrentCommandEncoder:] ``` or with exit 139 (SIGSEGV). The SIGABRT runs of the script above leave crash reports with `MTLReleaseAssertionFailure` and `arange_range_fill_mps` on the aborting thread. This is a SIGSEGV report from the same machine and the same two-thread `arange` workload, which shows the interleaving more clearly (symbol names only): ``` Thread 9 (queue 'metal gpu stream'), crashed: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV), KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x768 -[AGXG15XFamilyComputeContext setComputePipelineState:] invocation function for block in at::native::(anonymous namespace)::arange_range_fill_mps at::mps::dispatch_sync_with_rethrow at::native::(anonymous namespace)::arange_range_fill_mps <- at::native::arange_mps_out <- at::_ops::arange_start_out::call Thread 8: _dispatch_event_loop_wait_for_ownership <- _dispatch_sync_f_slow <- at::mps::dispatch_sync_with_rethrow <- at::native::(anonymous namespace)::arange_range_fill_mps <- at::native::arange_mps_out ``` A run of `torch.log` from two threads instead of `arange` (`Python-2026-09-19-223927.ips`) segfaults inside `std::unordered_map::emplace` called from `MetalShaderLibrary::exec_unary_kernel` on both threads. That one matches the race described in open PR #167541 (unguarded pipeline-state caches in `MetalShaderLibrary`). What I see in the source at 6f49d1f0287c449c186339782878346ad34847bd, the commit of the nightly above (may be a misreading; included so nobody has to look it up): - `arange_range_fill_mps` takes `stream->commandEncoder()` (`aten/src/ATen/native/mps/operations/RangeFactories.mm:34`) and `getPipelineStateForFunc(...)` (line 49) before entering `dispatch_sync_with_rethrow` (line 50). Another thread's `synchronize()` calls `endKernelCoalescing()`, which does `endEncoding` + `release` on that same encoder (`aten/src/ATen/mps/MPSStream.mm:135-141`). Other call sites take the encoder and the pipeline state inside the block (`OperationUtils.mm:1452-1458`). - PR #167541 adds a mutex around `libMap`/`cplMap` but does not change `RangeFactories.mm`. The `warmed` case of the attached `repro.py`, which runs every kernel once single-threaded before starting the threads, still crashes (3 / 3 on 2.14.0, 4 threads, 5 iters), so the arange crash does not look like a cache-population race alone. How I hit it: F5-TTS inference submits one forward pass per text batch to a `ThreadPoolExecutor` (`f5_tts/infer/utils_infer.py:553`), so two batches means two threads on MPS. If multi-threaded use of the MPS backend is not supported, a sentence saying so in the MPS notes would already help; I could not find one. Related: PR #167541 (open, no linked issue); #100285 (two threads calling `torch.nonzero`, same kind of Metal assertion, fixed for that one op by #108996); #78503 (the dispatch queue as the backend's threading model). ### Versions ``` PyTorch version: 2.14.0 Is debug build: False CUDA used to build PyTorch: None ROCM used to build PyTorch: N/A OS: macOS 26.5.1 (arm64) GCC version: Could not collect Clang version: 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101) CMake version: version 3.26.4 Libc version: N/A Python version: 3.11.5 (main, Aug 24 2023, 15:09:45) [Clang 14.0.3 (clang-1403.0.22.14.1)] (64-bit runtime) Python platform: macOS-26.5.1-arm64-arm-64bit Is CUDA available: False CUDA runtime version: No CUDA CUDA_MODULE_LOADING set to: N/A GPU models and configuration: No CUDA Nvidia driver version: No CUDA cuDNN driver version: No CUDA Is XPU available: False HIP runtime version: N/A MIOpen runtime version: N/A Is XNNPACK available: False Caching allocator config: N/A CPU: Apple M3 Pro Versions of relevant libraries: [pip3] Could not collect [conda] Could not collect ``` Also reproduced on `2.15.0.dev20260919` (commit 6f49d1f0287c449c186339782878346ad34847bd) in a second venv on the same machine, Python 3.11.5.
Full repro.py (the cases named above: threads_arange, serial, warmed) ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Minimal reproducer: PyTorch MPS crashes when >=2 Python threads run MPS ops concurrently. macOS 26 (Tahoe), Apple M-series. No F5-TTS, no model weights, no downloads. Root cause: MetalShaderLibrary's pipeline-state caches (libMap/cplMap/kernelCache, aten/src/ATen/native/mps/MetalShaderLibrary.h) are plain std::unordered_map with no mutex, and arange_range_fill_mps (aten/src/ATen/native/mps/operations/RangeFactories.mm:34,49) calls stream->commandEncoder() and getPipelineStateForFunc() OUTSIDE the serial queue, then uses the stale results inside the dispatch_sync_with_rethrow block. Real-world trigger: f5_tts/infer/utils_infer.py:553 submits one full MPS forward pass per text batch to a ThreadPoolExecutor. One batch => one thread => no crash; >=2 batches => crash. Usage: python repro.py --case threads_unary --threads 4 --iters 60 python repro.py --list """ from __future__ import annotations import argparse import sys import threading from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Tuple import torch DEV = "mps" UNARY: List[Tuple[str, Callable[[torch.Tensor], torch.Tensor]]] = [ ("log", torch.log), ("abs", torch.abs), ("exp", torch.exp), ("sqrt", torch.sqrt), ("sin", torch.sin), ("tanh", torch.tanh), ("erf", torch.erf), ("rsqrt", torch.rsqrt), ("log1p", torch.log1p), ("expm1", torch.expm1), ("log2", torch.log2), ("sinh", torch.sinh), ("atan", torch.atan), ("floor", torch.floor), ("sign", torch.sign), ("frac", torch.frac), ("lgamma", torch.lgamma), ("digamma", torch.digamma), ("i0", torch.i0), ("sinc", torch.sinc), ] DTYPES = [torch.float32, torch.float16, torch.bfloat16] def _combo(i: int) -> Tuple[str, Callable, torch.dtype, int]: """A (op, dtype, shape) triple that is new for every i -> forces a fresh pipeline compile.""" name, fn = UNARY[i % len(UNARY)] dt = DTYPES[(i // len(UNARY)) % len(DTYPES)] return name, fn, dt, 1 << (16 + (i % 6)) def hb(tag: str, i: int, msg: str = "") -> None: print(f"[{tag}] iter {i:03d} {msg}", flush=True) def w_unary(tag: str, iters: int) -> None: for i in range(iters): name, fn, dt, n = _combo(i) x = torch.rand(n, device=DEV, dtype=dt) + 0.5 hb(tag, i, f"{name}/{str(dt).split('.')[-1]}/{n} {float(fn(x).float().sum()):.3e}") def w_arange(tag: str, iters: int) -> None: for i in range(iters): dt = DTYPES[i % len(DTYPES)] a = torch.arange(0, 4096 + i, 1, device=DEV, dtype=dt) b = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, 2048 + i, device=DEV, dtype=dt) hb(tag, i, f"arange/{str(dt).split('.')[-1]} {float(a.float().sum() + b.float().sum()):.3e}") def w_graph(tag: str, iters: int) -> None: for i in range(iters): a = torch.randn(512, 512, device=DEV) c = torch.matmul(a, a) y = torch.nn.functional.conv1d(torch.randn(2, 64, 4096, device=DEV), torch.randn(64, 64, 3, device=DEV), padding=1) hb(tag, i, f"graph {float(c.sum() + y.sum()):.3e}") def w_forward(tag: str, iters: int) -> None: """One F5-shaped 'forward pass': a few Linears plus the unary/arange ops a sampler uses.""" m = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(256, 256), torch.nn.GELU(), torch.nn.Linear(256, 256)).to(DEV).eval() for i in range(iters): with torch.no_grad(): t = torch.arange(0, 256, device=DEV, dtype=torch.float32) / 256.0 h = m(torch.randn(4, 64, 256, device=DEV) + t) s = torch.log(h.abs() + 1e-5).sum() + torch.exp(h.clamp(max=5)).sum() hb(tag, i, f"fwd {float(s):.3e}") def run_threads(workers: List[Tuple[str, Callable[[str, int], None]]], iters: int) -> None: ts = [threading.Thread(target=fn, args=(tag, iters)) for tag, fn in workers] for t in ts: t.start() for t in ts: t.join() def case_threads_unary(n: int, iters: int) -> None: run_threads([(f"t{k}", w_unary) for k in range(n)], iters) def case_threads_arange(n: int, iters: int) -> None: run_threads([(f"t{k}", w_arange) for k in range(n)], iters) def case_threads_mixed(n: int, iters: int) -> None: run_threads([(f"t{k}", w_graph if k % 2 else w_unary) for k in range(n)], iters) def case_threads_f5_shape(n: int, iters: int) -> None: """Mirror of f5_tts/infer/utils_infer.py:553 - one forward pass per text batch, pooled.""" with ThreadPoolExecutor() as ex: list(ex.map(lambda k: w_forward(f"b{k}", iters), range(n))) def case_serial(n: int, iters: int) -> None: """CONTROL: identical total work, one thread. Must NOT crash.""" for k in range(n): w_unary(f"s{k}", iters) def case_serial_arange(n: int, iters: int) -> None: """CONTROL for threads_arange.""" for k in range(n): w_arange(f"s{k}", iters) def case_warmed(n: int, iters: int) -> None: """Pre-populate every pipeline-state cache single-threaded, THEN thread. Workaround test.""" w_unary("warm", iters) w_arange("warm", iters) run_threads([(f"t{k}", w_unary if k % 2 else w_arange) for k in range(n)], iters) CASES: Dict[str, Callable[[int, int], None]] = { "threads_unary": case_threads_unary, "threads_arange": case_threads_arange, "threads_mixed": case_threads_mixed, "threads_f5_shape": case_threads_f5_shape, "serial": case_serial, "serial_arange": case_serial_arange, "warmed": case_warmed, } def main() -> None: ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--case") ap.add_argument("--threads", type=int, default=4) ap.add_argument("--iters", type=int, default=60) ap.add_argument("--list", action="store_true") a = ap.parse_args() if a.list or not a.case: for k, f in CASES.items(): print(f"{k:18s} {(f.__doc__ or '').strip().splitlines()[0] if f.__doc__ else ''}") return print(f"torch={torch.__version__} case={a.case} threads={a.threads} iters={a.iters}", flush=True) CASES[a.case](a.threads, a.iters) torch.mps.synchronize() print("OK no crash", flush=True) sys.exit(0) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ```

title: [DTensor] Shard._select_split_tensor SymInt path computes a negative shard length for uneven splits
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Shard._select_split_tensor has a SymInt fast path (index is a torch.SymInt and with_padding=False) that assumes only the last shard is short and this branch is taken when index is not a Python int and with_padding=False.

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b6131af877449b1d3af5700b93b4a3bcbe8348fa/torch/distributed/tensor/placement_types.py#L281-L289

That is wrong when the first n-1 full chunks do not fit, for example when dim_size=5, num_chunks=4: 
- split_size=  (5 + 4 -1)//4 =2
-  last_split= ( 5 -2*(4-1))= -1
-  So the implied length is [2,2,2,-1] which is wrong.

The Python-int path (_split_tensor) returns [2, 2, 1, 0] as _custom_chunk already clamps this correctly:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b6131af877449b1d3af5700b93b4a3bcbe8348fa/torch/distributed/tensor/placement_types.py#L330-L336



### **Minimal repro:** 

```
python 

import torch
from torch.distributed.tensor import Shard
from torch.fx.experimental.symbolic_shapes import ShapeEnv

t = torch.arange(20).reshape(5, 4)
index = ShapeEnv().create_unbacked_symint()
Shard(0)._select_split_tensor(
    t,
    num_chunks=4,
    index=index,
    with_padding=False,
    clone=False,
    contiguous=False,
)

```

title: [inductor] x.index_put_(...) followed by x.add_(x.flip(0)): the copy back into x is fused with a read of x at other positions (silent wrong results, CUDA and CPU)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

An in-place update that reads the tensor at other positions, after an `index_put_` into the same tensor, gives wrong values under `torch.compile`. Either statement alone is fine.

```python
import torch


def f(x):
    x.index_put_((torch.arange(x.size(0), device=x.device),), x * 2.0)
    x.add_(x.flip(0))
    return x


device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
compiled = torch.compile(f)
for shape in ((4, 8), (1024, 2048)):
    x = torch.rand(*shape, device=device)
    want = f(x.clone())
    print(shape, [int((compiled(x.clone()) != want).sum()) for _ in range(5)])
```

CUDA, 2.14.0+cu130, RTX 4070 (2.9.1 is the same): right at the small shape, wrong at the large one.

```
(4, 8) [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
(1024, 2048) [1017616, 1020608, 1019568, 1020448, 1018848]
```

CPU, nightly 2.15.0.dev20260921: wrong at every size.

```
(4, 8) [16, 16, 16, 16, 16]
(1024, 2048) [1048576, 1048464, 1048576, 1048576, 1048576]
```

Same with `index_copy_`, `index_add_` or `x[idx] = ...` as the first statement, and with `x.copy_(x.flip(0))`, `x[1:] = x[:-1].clone()` or a foreach update as the second. With `x.mul_(2.0)` as the first statement it's right.

After reinplacing, `index_put_` writes `x` directly, and the flip and the add read `x` through the name of the index_put_ output. The copy back into `x` is then fused with them, so one kernel reads `x` at the flipped index while writing it:

```python
triton_poi_fused_add_copy__flip_1.run(arg0_1, arg0_1, 32, ...)
```

I think the check that should stop that is `Scheduler.fusable_weak_dep`. It looks for reads named `mutation_real_name[weak_dep.mutating_buf]` (`arg0_1`), but the reader reads `buf1` (the index_put_ output, whose real name is also `arg0_1`), so it finds no reads, skips the same-index check and allows the fusion. Resolving the read's name too:

```python
if self.mutation_real_name.get(read.name, read.name) == real_name
```

makes all of these right, CPU and CUDA. I'm running the Inductor tests against it and will send it.

title: LocalTensor] Finish permutation TODO in _prepare_collective_groups (keep order, mirror siblings)
body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Already listed as a TODO: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/distributed/_local_tensor/_c10d.py#L106-L110
``` python
    # TODO: We can handle permutations but the layout inference algorithm will
    # lose the permutation so we will have to reapply it
    if ranks != sorted(ranks):
        raise AssertionError(ranks)
    offset = ranks[0]
    ranks = [r - offset for r in ranks]

    shape, strides = _indices_to_layout(ranks)
    layout = _FlatLayout(shape, strides)

    global_pg = _get_default_group()
    group_offsets = layout.complement(global_pg.size()).all_ranks_from_zero()

    return ranks, group_offsets, offset
```


Proposal:   We should keep using sorted ranks for layout/complement (finding sibling sets), but return the original rank list and build every fiber in that order so group-local ranks match the caller's PG. We should apply the same list to every sibling base, mirroring order across fibers (for SPMD consistency), rather than leaving siblings sorted.

For example:     PG ranks = [4, 7, 5, 6], world_size= 12
                            m = min(ranks)                              # 4
                            sorted(ranks) -> [4, 5, 6, 7] for layout and complement
                              sibling bases o = [0, 4, 8]
                            rel = [r - m for r in ranks]                # [0, 3, 1, 2]  
                            for o in [0, 4, 8]:
                                fiber = [o + x for x in rel]              
                                # o=0: [0, 3, 1, 2]
                                                                                        # o=4: [4, 7, 5, 6]   # visible_pg(maintains permutation)
                                                                                       # o=8: [8, 11, 9, 10]


Basically the reapply approach the TODO asks to do.

Why it matters: I think it’s worth closing this gap.  Since torch.distributed.new_group(..., sort_ranks=False) preserves the caller’s rank order, and get_process_group_ranks returns ranks in that group-local order. LocalTensor’s _prepare_collective_groups still asserts if that list isn’t sorted, so a group like new_group( [4, 7, 5, 6] , sort_ranks=False) cannot run under LocalTensorMode.

Happy to send a PR if this approach seems fine!

title: [inductor] x.copy_(x.transpose(-1, -2) * 1.0) on CUDA: a weak dep pruned before loop reordering lets the copy fuse with a transposed read (silent wrong results, regression)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Transposing a batch of matrices in place gives wrong values under `torch.compile` on CUDA at some sizes. Eager is fine, and so is 2.9.1.

```python
import torch


def f(x):
    x.copy_(x.transpose(-1, -2) * 1.0)
    return x


compiled = torch.compile(f)
for shape in ((652, 5, 5), (80000, 5, 5), (64, 256, 256)):
    x = torch.rand(*shape, device="cuda")
    want = f(x.clone())
    print(shape, [int((compiled(x.clone()) != want).sum()) for _ in range(5)])
```

2.14.0+cu130, RTX 4070:

```
(652, 5, 5) [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
(80000, 5, 5) [2499, 13060, 13165, 13558, 13757]
(64, 256, 256) [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
```

(the last shape gives 3,000 to 4,000 wrong in other runs). Same with `x[:] = x.transpose(-1, -2).clone()`, `x.copy_(x.transpose(-1, -2).contiguous())` and `x.copy_(x.mT.clone())`. With `torch._inductor.config.loop_ordering_after_fusion = False` it's right, which I think is why 2.9.1 is.

In the pre-fusion IR, op0 computes the transposed value and reads `arg0_1` at the natural index; op1 is the copy back into `arg0_1` (buf1, a mutation of arg0_1), reads buf0 at the transposed index, and has `WeakDep(name='buf0', mutating_buf='buf1')`. `_prune_redundant_deps` drops that weak dep, because op1 also has a MemoryDep on buf0 and `fusable_weak_dep` sees op0 read `arg0_1` at the index op1 writes it. Then `shared_data_after_reordering_loop` reorders op0's loops so that its write of buf0 matches op1's read, and that moves op0's read of `arg0_1` to the transposed index too. Nothing checks the mutation again, and the fused kernel reads `arg0_1` transposed while writing it:

```
triton_poi_fused_copy_copy__mul_0.run(arg0_1, arg0_1, 400000, 5, stream=raw_stream0)
```

Not reordering the loops of a pair where one node mutates a buffer the other reads makes all of these right. Would you rather have that, or the pruned weak deps checked again after a reorder? I can send either.

title: torch.compile: isinstance(x, ProtoA | ProtoB) silently returns False for runtime_checkable Protocols with non-method members
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Under `torch.compile`, `isinstance(obj, A | B)` and `isinstance(obj, (A, B))` silently return `False` where eager returns `True`, when one of the members is a `runtime_checkable` `Protocol` with a **non-method (data) member**. There is no graph break and no warning — `fullgraph=True` compiles happily and the traced code takes the wrong branch.

The single-class form `isinstance(obj, A)` is correct, so the divergence appears only when the protocol is combined with anything else. It is also **order dependent**: the wrong answer is produced only when the data-member protocol is reached during evaluation, so swapping the operands can mask it.

```python
from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable

import torch


@runtime_checkable
class HasPorts(Protocol):          # non-method (data) member
    ports: tuple[int, ...]


@runtime_checkable
class HasFoo(Protocol):            # method member
    def foo(self) -> int: ...


class Obj:
    ports = (1, 2)

    def foo(self) -> int:
        return 1


def single(o):     return isinstance(o, HasPorts)
def union(o):      return isinstance(o, HasPorts | HasFoo)
def tup(o):        return isinstance(o, (HasPorts, HasFoo))
def union_rev(o):  return isinstance(o, HasFoo | HasPorts)
def workaround(o): return isinstance(o, HasPorts) or isinstance(o, HasFoo)


for fn in (single, union, tup, union_rev, workaround):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    eager = fn(Obj())
    compiled = torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(Obj())
    print(f"{fn.__name__:<11} eager={eager!s:<6} compiled={compiled!s:<6} "
          f"{'' if eager == compiled else '  <-- WRONG'}")
```

Output on 2.14.0:

```
single      eager=True   compiled=True
union       eager=True   compiled=False    <-- WRONG
tup         eager=True   compiled=False    <-- WRONG
union_rev   eager=True   compiled=True
workaround  eager=True   compiled=True
```

`backend="eager"` is used to show this is a Dynamo-level issue; `"inductor"` behaves the same.

### Root cause

`BuiltinVariable.call_isinstance` in `torch/_dynamo/variables/builtin.py` has two paths.

The single-class path delegates to the real hook, which is why `single` is correct:

```python
if (
    isinstance(arg, variables.UserDefinedObjectVariable)
    and "__instancecheck__" in isinstance_type.__class__.__dict__
):
    return VariableTracker.build(
        tx, isinstance_type.__class__.__instancecheck__(isinstance_type, arg.value)
    )
```

For a `Protocol`, `isinstance_type.__class__` is `typing._ProtocolMeta`, which defines `__instancecheck__`, so the branch is taken.

For a union or tuple, `isinstance_type.__class__` is `types.UnionType` or `tuple`, neither of which defines `__instancecheck__`, so the branch is skipped and control reaches:

```python
try:
    val = issubclass(arg_type, isinstance_type_tuple)
except TypeError:
    val = arg_type in isinstance_type_tuple
return VariableTracker.build(tx, val)
```

`issubclass()` is not equivalent to `isinstance()` here. A `runtime_checkable` protocol with a data member explicitly refuses it:

```
>>> issubclass(Obj, HasPorts)
TypeError: Protocols with non-method members don't support issubclass().
           Non-method members: 'ports'.
```

That `TypeError` is caught, and the fallback `arg_type in isinstance_type_tuple` compares the *class object* by identity against the tuple members — `Obj in (HasPorts, HasFoo)` — which is `False` for any real program. So a `TypeError` that means "I cannot answer this way" is converted into a confident `False`.

The order dependence follows from `issubclass()` short-circuiting left to right: with `(HasFoo, HasPorts)` the method protocol matches first and it never reaches the one that raises, so that spelling happens to be correct.

### Suggested fix

Let the union/tuple case use the same delegation the single-class case already uses — normalize to a tuple of members first, then, if any member's metaclass defines `__instancecheck__`, answer with `any(...)` over the real hooks. Failing that, the `except TypeError` fallback should graph break rather than answer `False`, since at that point Dynamo has established it cannot compute the predicate.

### Workarounds

Both of these compile to the correct answer today, and are what we shipped:

```python
# 1. Ask one protocol at a time and combine in Python.
drivable = isinstance(layer, DrivableLayer)
resumable = isinstance(layer, ResumableLayer)
if not drivable and not resumable:
    ...

# 2. Or give the protocol only method members, which keeps issubclass() usable.
@runtime_checkable
class HasPorts(Protocol):
    def get_ports(self) -> tuple[int, ...]: ...
```

Ordering the members so a method-only protocol comes first also happens to work, but it is a coincidence of the short-circuit rather than something to rely on.

### Why this bites

The failure is a silent wrong branch inside a compiled region, not an exception, so it surfaces far from its cause. In our case a capability check on a layer object rejected every layer once the surrounding step was compiled, while the identical check passed in eager and in every unit test that did not compile. Non-method members are the normal way to express "this object exposes attribute X" in a structural protocol, and `A | B` is the natural spelling for "either capability", so the combination is not exotic.

### Versions

torch 2.14.0+cpu, Python 3.14.2, Linux (WSL2). Also reproduces with `backend="inductor"`.

*How did we mitigate the issue?*

Possible mitigation: move B200 back from trunk to unstable again, given its issue frequency. 

## Prevention/followups
*How do we prevent issues like this in the future?*

When admin powers the node back online, the provision scripts should either not run, or need to pass certain verification before it is added back to github.

title: [Test] `test_linalg.py` failures when CUDA profiling runs after CPU-only profiling
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I'm seeing failures in `test_call_count_tunableop_cuda_float32` due to other tests (for example, `test_matmul_folds_viewable`) registering Kineto with CPU-only profiling before this test gets called. The profiler therefore does not see the three CUDA kernels that run and reports 0. This problem has appeared before in `test_profiler.py` and was fixed by #186970, which registers both CPU and CUDA profiler activity during setup. The same fix works for `test_linalg.py`. 

Given that this problem is now appearing in multiple places, a few questions:
1. Does it make sense to reconsider how Kineto registration works? From a different perspective, is calling the profiler multiple times in the same process with different profiler activities considered a supported use case?
2. Should the profiler notify users somehow if the requested profiling modes are not supported by the existing registration?
3. Is the test-side solution implemented by #186970 the "blessed" path for now? If so, the quickest fix would be to move the Kineto setup to one of the test util files and import/use it both in `test_profiler.py` and `test_linalg.py`.

title: [MPS] `bmm` silently returns wrong results when the output exceeds 2**32 elements and an input is non-contiguous
body:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

On macOS 15+, `torch.bmm` on MPS silently returns wrong values when the output has more than 2**32 elements and either input is a non-contiguous view, e.g. a transposed `k` in attention (`q @ k.transpose(-1, -2)`). No error or warning is raised. With contiguous inputs the same shapes are correct.

The shapes involved are realistic: attention scores `(B*H, L, L)` exceed 2**32 elements at, e.g., 32 heads × 4k context × batch 9. The case most likely to go unnoticed is batched feature extraction or probing on Apple Silicon, and attention-map analysis with `output_attentions=True` (which forces eager attention). There the corrupted activations can look like a mildly worse downstream metric rather than an obvious failure.

The reference in the script below is the CPU result for the same batch element.

```python
import torch

torch.manual_seed(0)
L, D = 256, 64
for B in (65536 - 16, 65536 + 16):  # output numel crosses 2**32 at B = 65536
    q = torch.randn(B, L, D, device="mps")
    k = torch.randn(B, L, D, device="mps")
    out = torch.bmm(q, k.transpose(1, 2))  # batch2 is a transposed (non-contiguous) view
    for i in (0, B - 1):
        ref = q[i].cpu() @ k[i].cpu().T
        err = ((out[i].cpu() - ref).abs().max() / ref.abs().max()).item()
        print(f"B={B} numel/2**32={B * L * L / 2**32:.4f} batch={i} rel_err={err:.2e}")
    del q, k, out
    torch.mps.empty_cache()
```

Output (torch 2.14.0, macOS 27.0, M2 Ultra):

```
B=65520 numel/2**32=0.9998 batch=0 rel_err=0.00e+00
B=65520 numel/2**32=0.9998 batch=65519 rel_err=0.00e+00
B=65552 numel/2**32=1.0002 batch=0 rel_err=1.51e+00
B=65552 numel/2**32=1.0002 batch=65551 rel_err=1.49e+00
```

Additional observations:

- Wrong results with a transposed `batch2` reproduce on torch 2.11.0, 2.12.1, 2.13.0 and 2.14.0. They appear at every batch index checked (0, 1, 32767, 65535, 65536, 65537, last), not only in the last tile.
- With `.contiguous()` inputs the same shape is correct on 2.11.0, 2.12.1 and 2.14.0 (rel_err 0). On 2.13.0 the contiguous case segfaults instead, which looks like a separate problem that 2.14.0 fixed.
- A non-contiguous `batch1` also gives wrong results on 2.14.0, and segfaults on 2.11.0.
- On 2.11.0–2.13.0, a later large `bmm` in the same process can segfault after the wrong-result call, so the strided read may also go out of bounds.
- The same failure reaches 4-D `torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-1, -2))`, i.e. eager attention in HF `transformers` (found with DistilBERT, `(B, H, L, L) = (5712, 12, 256, 256)`).
- On macOS < 15 this shape raises `Tiling of batch matmul for larger than 2**32 entries only available from MacOS15 onwards`, so upgrading the OS turns a hard error into silently wrong output.

### Likely cause

`bmm_out_mps_impl` sends outputs larger than 2**32 elements to `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` (`aten/src/ATen/native/mps/operations/LinearAlgebra.mm`). That function takes the raw buffers via `getMTLBufferStorage` and builds `MPSNDArrayDescriptor`s from sizes alone, assuming a packed row-major layout. It never looks at the input strides. The code that materialises transposed views (`if (batch2.is_view() && !batch2.is_contiguous())`) runs only on macOS < 15, on the assumption that the strided kernels handle views on macOS 15+. The tiled path does not go through those kernels. The same structure is still on `main` as of 2026-09-16 (1943e23e).

A likely fix is to call `.contiguous()` on `batch1` and `batch2` before `tiled_bmm_out_mps_impl` (the call site already does `resolve_conj()`), or to raise an error for non-contiguous inputs.

## Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0 (also reproduced on 2.11.0, 2.12.1, 2.13.0)
OS: macOS 27.0 (arm64)
Python version: 3.13.9
CPU: Apple M2 Ultra (192 GB unified memory)
```

title: Migrate remaining VariableTrackers to declarative `tp_methods` / `tp_getset` / `tp_members`
body:
### Disclaimer

Some of the action items are good candidates for a "good first issue". It is a mechanical refactor of existing code, and any LLM can assist with it.

**No need to ask for permission to work on this issue**. Just make sure no one else is working on it.

### Background

Dynamo is moving `VariableTracker` (VT) method and attribute dispatch off ad-hoc `call_method` / `var_getattr` `if name == "..."` chains and onto the declarative class-level tables in `torch/_dynamo/variables/base.py`:

- `tp_methods: dict[str, Method]` — analogous to CPython `PyMethodDef`. Handler signature `(self, tx, args, kwargs) -> VT | None`; returning `None` declines and falls through to object-protocol dispatch. Arity is auto-derived from the real CPython method's `ml_flags`.
- `tp_getset` / `tp_members` — analogous to `PyGetSetDef` / `PyMemberDef`.

Lookup walks the MRO (`_lookup_tp_table`), so subclass tables add to inherited entries. Dispatch is consumed by `VariableTracker.call_method` and `tp_getattro_impl` in `base.py`. The `var_getattr` override has already been fully eliminated across `variables/*.py`; the remaining old pattern lives in `call_method` overrides. Reference migration: commit `a61f50d` (UserDefinedExceptionVariable).

### Why do this migration

1. **Automatic argument checking.** `Method` derives arity flags from the real CPython method's `ml_flags` and runs a centralized arity check
2. **Unifies and simplifies attribute dispatch (`tp_getattro` / `tp_setattro`).**
3. **MRO-aware, composable inheritance.**
4. **Mirrors CPython's own type model.** `PyMethodDef` / `PyGetSetDef` / `PyMemberDef` semantics are well understood
5. **Single source of truth / less bug surface.** Methods and attributes are enumerable in one big table

**Out of scope:** single-branch `__setattr__` / `__new__` / `__delattr__` branches — these are the `tp_setattro` / `tp_new` slots and are intentionally not routed through `tp_methods` (see comment near `user_defined.py:4429`).

### Candidates

Small / self-contained (good first issues):

- [x] `AutogradEngineVariable` (#195175)
- [x] `OptimizerVariable` (#195173)
- [x] `DispatchKeySetVariable` (#195168) - in progress
- [x] `FuncTorchInterpreterVariable` (#195171) - in progress
- [x] `ContextVarVariable` (#195167) - in progress
- [x] `AutogradFunctionVariable` (#195180)
- [x] `AutogradFunctionContextVariable` (#195179)
- [ ] `BaseBuiltinVariable` (#195177) - in progress

Medium:

- [x] `NNModuleVariable` (#195193) - in progress
- [ ] `NumpyNdarrayVariable` (#195473) - in progress - (has a generic method wrapper that
      resists a purely declarative conversion)
- [x] `DictBuiltinVariable` (#195181)
- [x] `ListBuiltinVariable`


Large / complex (defer) - **Do not work on those**:

- [ ] `ConstantVariable` —  (not trivial because it can represent multiple types, but still self-contained)
- [ ] `BuiltinVariable` — (all arithmetic/comparison dunders)
- [ ] `UserDefinedObjectVariable`
- [ ] `UserDefinedClassVariable`
- [ ] `TensorVariable`
- [ ] `SymNodeVariable`

~Follow-on: the 26 remaining `tp_getattro_impl` overrides that branch on `name` internally are candidates for `tp_getset` / `tp_members` conversion.~

### Notes

- Handlers should return `None` (not call `super()`) to decline; base `call_method` handles fall-through.
- Do not hand-roll arity checks — `Method` derives them from `ml_flags`.

title: AOTInductor drops the storage offset of a mutable view argument under dynamic shapes (missing lowering for aten.sym_storage_offset)
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When a custom operator declares a mutable argument (`mutates_args=...`, i.e. a `Tensor(a!)` in the schema) and that argument is a **view of a larger buffer**, AOTInductor drops the view's storage offset under **dynamic shapes**. Every write lands at the start of the base buffer instead of at the view's offset.

There is no error or warning. The compiled model just returns wrong numbers, so it looks like a numerical problem in the model rather than a compiler issue.

Static export is unaffected, and so is `torch.compile` with the default Python wrapper. Only dynamic-shape AOTInductor is wrong.

#### Repro

Reproduces on **CPU and CUDA**, so no GPU is needed.

```python
"""AOTInductor drops the storage offset of a mutable (Tensor(a!)) view argument
under dynamic shapes.

    python repro.py         # cuda
    python repro.py cpu     # cpu
"""
import sys
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.export import Dim
from torch._inductor import aoti_compile_and_package
from torch._inductor.package import load_package

DEV = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "cuda"


@torch.library.custom_op("repro::write", mutates_args=("out",))
def write(out: torch.Tensor, x: torch.Tensor) -> None:
    out.copy_(x)


@write.register_fake
def _(out, x):
    return None


class M(nn.Module):
    """Two mutable writes into two disjoint slices of one zeroed buffer."""

    def forward(self, x0, x1):
        n0, n1 = x0.shape[0], x1.shape[0]
        buf = torch.zeros(n0 * 8 + n1 * 8, dtype=x0.dtype, device=x0.device)
        v0 = buf[: n0 * 8].view(n0, 8)      # storage_offset 0
        v1 = buf[n0 * 8 :].view(n1, 8)      # storage_offset n0*8, symbolic
        torch.ops.repro.write(v0, x0)
        torch.ops.repro.write(v1, x1)
        return v0.sum(), v1.sum()


def main():
    m = M().eval()
    xs = (torch.ones(10, 8, device=DEV), torch.full((5, 8), 2.0, device=DEV))
    expected = tuple(t.item() for t in m(*xs))          # (80.0, 80.0)

    for label, dynamic_shapes in (
        ("static ", None),
        ("dynamic", ({0: Dim("n0", min=2, max=64)}, {0: Dim("n1", min=2, max=64)})),
    ):
        ep = torch.export.export(m, xs, dynamic_shapes=dynamic_shapes)
        pkg = aoti_compile_and_package(ep, package_path=f"/tmp/repro_{label.strip()}.pt2")
        got = tuple(t.item() for t in load_package(pkg)(*xs))
        print(f"{label}  expected={expected}  aoti={got}  {'OK' if got == expected else 'WRONG'}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(f"torch {torch.__version__}  device {DEV}")
    main()
```

#### Output

```
torch 2.14.0+cu130  device cuda
static   expected=(80.0, 80.0)  aoti=(80.0, 80.0)  OK
dynamic  expected=(80.0, 80.0)  aoti=(120.0, 0.0)  WRONG

torch 2.14.0+cu130  device cpu
static   expected=(80.0, 80.0)  aoti=(80.0, 80.0)  OK
dynamic  expected=(80.0, 80.0)  aoti=(120.0, 0.0)  WRONG
```

Both writes went to the first slice: it sums to 120 instead of 80, and the second slice was never written, so it sums to 0.

#### Root cause

`aten.sym_storage_offset` has no Inductor lowering.

1. Functionalization turns the mutating call into `auto_functionalized_v2`, recording the mutated view as a base plus its size, stride and storage offset.
2. The re-inplacing pass rebuilds the view as `as_strided(base, size, stride, sym_storage_offset(view))`. The post-grad FX graph is correct at this point, e.g.

   ```
   sym_storage_offset_default: "Sym(16384*(((s4 + 255)//256)))" = torch.ops.aten.sym_storage_offset.default(slice_2)
   as_strided_default = torch.ops.aten.as_strided.default(full, [...], [64, 1], sym_storage_offset_default)
   ```
3. `aten.sym_storage_offset.default` is not in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`, while its siblings `sym_size.int`, `sym_stride.int` and `sym_numel` all are. Those exist precisely so the value is read from the node's metadata instead of being recomputed.
4. So it takes the implicit fallback, which re-executes the op on tensors rebuilt by `ir_node_to_tensor()`. That helper allocates with `torch.empty_strided(size, stride, ...)`, copying size and stride from the layout but never the offset, so every rebuilt tensor reports `storage_offset() == 0`.
5. The node lowers to the integer `0`, `as_strided` builds a `ReinterpretView` at offset 0, and the generated C++ passes `0L`:

   ```cpp
   // mutable argument, dynamic build
   reinterpret_tensor_wrapper(buf0, 2, int_array_2, int_array_1, 0L)
   // read-only argument in the same call, correct
   reinterpret_tensor_wrapper(buf0, 2, int_array_2, int_array_1,
                              16384L*c10::div_floor_integer(255L + s33, 256L))
   ```

Static export escapes this because the offset is a constant that never becomes a node. The default Python wrapper escapes it because the mutation stays in place and no `as_strided` is emitted.

Instrumenting the lowering shows the node's metadata is right and the lowered value is not:

```
[run_node] sym_storage_offset_default: meta_val=16384*(((s4 + 255)//256))  ->  lowered=0 (int)
```

#### Suggested fix

Register the missing lowering next to its siblings in `torch/_inductor/lowering.py`:

```python
@register_lowering(aten.sym_storage_offset.default)
def sym_storage_offset(a):
    val = V.graph.current_node.meta["val"]
    if isinstance(val, torch.SymInt):
        return val.node.expr
    else:
        return int(val)
```

With that patch applied, the repro above prints `OK` for both static and dynamic on CPU and CUDA. It also fixes a real model where several accumulator buffers are packed into one allocation and each consumer is handed its own slice.

A PR with this fix and a regression test in `test/inductor/test_aot_inductor.py` follows.

### Versions

Reproduced on 2.11.0+cu130, 2.13.0+cu130 and 2.14.0+cu130, on both CPU and CUDA (B200, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12 and 3.14).

`torch/_inductor/lowering.py` on `main` registers `sym_size.int`, `sym_stride.int` and `sym_numel`, and contains no occurrence of `sym_storage_offset`, so `main` looks affected as well.

title: [TorchInductor] Lite mode skips Triton wrapper decomposition in nested subgraphs, causing compilation failure
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

## Summary

`torch.compile(mode="lite")` fails when a naturally captured `torch.cond` subgraph contains a `triton_kernel_wrapper_functional` node.

The default configuration successfully decomposes the wrapper and compiles the same model. Lite mode disables post-grad passes, but its correctness decomposition checks only the root graph and returns before visiting the subgraph.

The undecomposed wrapper reaches Inductor lowering and causes a compilation failure.

## Reproducer

```python
import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


@triton.jit
def add_one_kernel(in_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(0)
    offsets = pid * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    values = tl.load(in_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, values + 1, mask=mask)


class AddOne(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    def forward(ctx, value):
        output = torch.empty_like(value)
        add_one_kernel[(value.numel(),)](
            value, output, value.numel(), BLOCK_SIZE=4
        )
        return output

    @staticmethod
    def backward(ctx, grad):
        return grad


def model(x):
    def true_branch(value):
        return (AddOne.apply(value),)

    def false_branch(value):
        return (value.clone(),)

    return torch.cond(torch.tensor(True), true_branch, false_branch, (x,))[0]


x = torch.randn(4, 4, device="cuda", requires_grad=True)

# Succeeds.
torch.compile(model, backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)(x)

# Fails.
torch.compile(model, backend="inductor", mode="lite", fullgraph=True)(x)
```

## Observed behavior

AOT FX capture produces a root graph with no functional wrapper and a `true_graph_0` subgraph containing one.

With the default configuration, the wrapper is decomposed (1 → 0) and compilation succeeds. 

With `mode="lite"`, the wrapper remains (1 → 1) and compilation fails.

Directly setting `use_post_grad_passes=False` reproduces the same failure.

The failing configurations raise:

```text
LoweringException:
AssertionError: triton_kernel_wrapper_functional is not an OpOverload
```



## Root cause

In `compile_fx.py::_recursive_post_grad_passes`
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f07882e293662058329c946feb5615b1aaeedb82/torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py#L725-L763
the `use_post_grad_passes=False` branch checks the current graph for functional Triton wrappers and then returns. It does not recurse into the `get_attr` subgraphs.

The root graph contains no wrapper, while `true_graph_0` contains one. Therefore, the required decomposition is never invoked for `true_graph_0`, and the wrapper reaches Inductor lowering.

`mode="lite"`
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/f07882e293662058329c946feb5615b1aaeedb82/torch/_inductor/__init__.py#L306-L342 is a built-in compilation mode whose options include `"use_post_grad_passes": False`

### Versions

PyTorch main revision: `f07882e`

title: [symm_mem] Signal-pad slots collide across process groups where a signal sent in one group completes a wait in another
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

a symmetric-memory allocation has one signal pad shared by every process group that rendezvouses on it. The allocator caches a separate handle for each group on the same block https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b54e2abd0607ebe621336cfcaad9d63bc8f16bd6/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L934-L946 but those handles map the same allocation-resident signal pads pad mapping https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b54e2abd0607ebe621336cfcaad9d63bc8f16bd6/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L788-L802 the destination pad is selected through the group's `signal_pads` table, while the offset within that pad is only
`world_size * channel + rank` (or `src_rank`). Here `world_size` and the source rank are group-local; no unique group identifier is included put_signal
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b54e2abd0607ebe621336cfcaad9d63bc8f16bd6/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L200-L210 wait_signal https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b54e2abd0607ebe621336cfcaad9d63bc8f16bd6/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory.cu#L257-L266

two groups with different memberships can therefore map *different senders* onto the *same physical slot*. `wait_signal()` on one group's handle can be completed by a `put_signal()` issued on another group's handle, i.e. the waiter observes a signal from a rank that never signaled it. The failure is silent: no error, wrong synchronization.

Concrete aliasing example (3 ranks):

- WORLD (world_size 3): `wait_signal(src_rank=1, channel=0)` reads slot `3*0 + 1 = 1` of the local pad.
- Subgroup `[0, 2]` (world_size 2): `put_signal(dst_rank=0, channel=0)` from group-local rank 1 (= global rank 2) writes slot `2*0 + 1 = 1` of global rank 0's pad — the same slot.

So global rank 2's subgroup signal is consumed as if it were a WORLD signal from global rank 1.

### Repro

```python
# torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=3 repro.py
import os, time
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed._symmetric_memory as symm_mem

rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])
torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
dist.init_process_group("nccl")
group_b = dist.new_group([0, 2])

t = symm_mem.empty(64, device=f"cuda:{rank}")
# WORLD is rendezvoused first by all ranks; see the companion StoreExchange
# issue for why interleaving subgroup-only rendezvous would deadlock instead.
hdl_w = symm_mem.rendezvous(t, dist.group.WORLD)
if rank in (0, 2):
    hdl_b = symm_mem.rendezvous(t, group_b)
dist.barrier()

if rank == 2:
    hdl_b.put_signal(dst_rank=0)  # writes slot 1 of rank 0's pad
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
dist.barrier()

if rank == 0:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    # Global rank 1 never signals, so this must time out after 5s.
    hdl_w.wait_signal(src_rank=1, timeout_ms=5000)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    print(f"wait_signal returned after {time.perf_counter() - t0:.4f}s")
dist.barrier()
```

Observed on 3x H200 (NVLink), CUDA backend:

```
wait_signal returned after 0.0032s
```

expected: ~5s timeout followed by the device-side trap. The WORLD wait was completed by the subgroup put.

`barrier()` aliases the same way: its shared kernel uses the same within-pad offset with group-local ranks https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/b54e2abd0607ebe621336cfcaad9d63bc8f16bd6/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/symm_mem/CUDASymmetricMemory-inl.cuh#L138-L162 Concurrent barriers on overlapping groups can therefore consume each other's flags and complete before all members arrive.

### Affected backends

The collision is present in the CUDA backend's `put_signal()`, `wait_signal()`, and shared `barrier()` kernel. The NCCL backend also uses the shared barrier (#188051). The NVSHMEM backend will use the same shared signal kernels once #191858's fix lands, and its one-pad-per allocation model intentionally matches the CUDA backend.

title: [symm_mem]: rendezvous on a subgroup hangs a later rendezvous on a larger group
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`symm_mem.rendezvous()` on a process group that excludes some ranks leaves the
ranks with mismatched store-exchange sequence numbers. A later rendezvous on a
group that includes the excluded ranks then hangs forever.

This is on the default path and needs no special hardware or topology, only a
group that is not a partition of the world.

Repro (needs 3+ GPUs so a subgroup can exclude a rank):

```python
# torchrun --nproc_per_node=3 repro.py
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed._symmetric_memory as symm_mem

rank = int(os.environ["RANK"])
world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
dist.init_process_group("nccl")

sub_ranks = list(range(world_size - 1))  # excludes the last rank
subgroup = dist.new_group(sub_ranks)

if rank in sub_ranks:
    a = symm_mem.empty(64, device=f"cuda:{rank}")
    symm_mem.rendezvous(a, subgroup)
dist.barrier()
if rank == 0:
    print("STEP1 ok: rendezvous on the subgroup", flush=True)

b = symm_mem.empty(64, device=f"cuda:{rank}")
symm_mem.rendezvous(b, dist.group.WORLD)
if rank == 0:
    print("STEP2 ok: rendezvous on WORLD", flush=True)

dist.destroy_process_group()
```

Expected: both steps print.
Actual: `STEP1` prints, `STEP2` never does, all ranks block inside `rendezvous`.

### Cause

`StoreExchange` builds store keys as `"<prefix>/<seq_id>/<rank>"` and bumps a
single process-global `seq_id_` per exchange
(`CUDASymmetricMemoryUtils.hpp`), and the CUDA backend has one static
instance:

```cpp
static StoreExchange storeExchange = StoreExchange("CUDASymmetricMemory");
```

`make_peer_alloc_info` runs several exchanges per rendezvous. On a subgroup
rendezvous only the participating ranks run them, so the excluded ranks' counter
falls behind. The next rendezvous including those ranks has each side deriving a
different key, and it blocks.

title: [v2.14.1] Release Tracker
body:
This issue is for tracking cherry-picks to the release branch. Following is [release branch](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/release/2.14) for the 2.14.1 release.

Our plan from this point is roughly the following:

* Phase 1 (until 9/25): Cherry-pick post deadline (End of day 5PM PST)
* Phase 2 (after 9/25):  Perform extended integration/stability/performance testing based on Release Candidate builds.

**Only issues that have ‘cherry-picks’ in this tracker will be considered for the release.**

## Cherry-Pick Criteria

**Phase 1 (until 9/25):**

Please note: **No feature work allowed for cherry picks**. The Releng team relies on the cherry pick process to manage risk to release quality, i.e. by porting a small set of commit from trunk that are "must-have" into the release branch, we limit the change to the minimal to address pressing issues. Thus, not everything a developer land into the trunk will make it into the release. So, please consider the criteria below and follow the cherry picking process. Only low-risk changes may be cherry-picked from master:

1. Fixes to regressions against the most recent release (e.g. 2.14.0 for 2.14.1 release; see [module: regression issue list](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22module%3A+regression%22+))
2. Low risk critical fixes for: silent correctness, backwards compatibility, crashes, deadlocks, (large) memory leaks
3. Critical Fixes to new features being introduced in 2.14.0 release
4. Documentation improvements
5. Release branch specific changes (e.g. blocking ci fixes, change version identifiers)


Any other change requires special dispensation from the release managers (currently @atalman, @huydhn, @malfet). If this applies to your change please write "Special Dispensation" in the "Criteria Category:" template below and explain. 

**Phase 2 (after 9/25):**

Note that changes here require us to rebuild a Release Candidate and restart extended testing (likely delaying the release). Therefore, the only accepted changes are **Release-blocking** critical fixes for: [silent correctness](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+correctness+%28silent%29%22), [backwards compatibility](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+bc-breaking%22+), [crashes](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+crash%22+), [deadlocks](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+deadlock%22+), (large) [memory leaks](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3A%22topic%3A+memory+usage%22+)

Changes will likely require a discussion with the larger release team over VC or Slack.

## Cherry-Pick Process

1. Ensure your PR has landed in master. This does not apply for release-branch specific changes (see Phase 1 criteria).
2. Create (but do not land) a PR against the [release branch](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/tree/release/2.14).
   <details>

    ```bash
    # Find the hash of the commit you want to cherry pick
    # (for example, abcdef12345)
    git log

    git fetch origin release/2.14
    git checkout release/2.14
    git cherry-pick abcdef12345

    # Submit a PR based against 'release/2.14' either:
    # via the GitHub UI
    git push my-fork

    # via the GitHub CLI
    gh pr create --base release/2.14
    ```

    </details>
3. Make a request below with the following format:

```
Link to landed trunk PR (if applicable):
* 

Link to release branch PR:
* 

Criteria Category:
* 
```

1. Someone from the release team will reply with approved / denied or ask for more information.
2. If approved, someone from the release team will merge your PR once the tests pass. **Do not land the release branch PR yourself.**

**NOTE: Our normal tools (ghstack / ghimport, etc.) do not work on the release branch.**

See [HUD 2.14](https://hud.pytorch.org/hud/pytorch/pytorch/release%2F2.14/1?per_page=50)

```
        to_dtype_9 = ops.to_dtype(to_dtype_8, torch.bfloat16)
        to_dtype_10 = ops.to_dtype(to_dtype_9, torch.float32, src_dtype = torch.bfloat16, use_compute_types = False)
        get_index_1 = self.get_index('index3')
        index_expr = ops.index_expr(get_index_1, torch.float32)
        constant_1 = ops.constant(-9.210340371976184, torch.float32)
        mul_1 = ops.mul(index_expr, constant_1)
        constant_2 = ops.constant(0.0078125, torch.float32)
        mul_2 = ops.mul(mul_1, constant_2)
        exp = ops.exp(mul_2)
        mul_3 = ops.mul(to_dtype_10, exp)
        cos = ops.cos(mul_3)
        return cos
```

It showed to be the common problem of the triton code generation backend. Although I am running on XPU, it should be able to reproduce in CUDA GPU.

We found that running on CPU, the same ir_pre_fusion.txt with duplicates exists. But we saw cpp.py code generation has a loop body pass to eliminate such duplicates. But on triton code generation, this doesn't exist.

Steps to reproduce:
[repro_time_text_embed_compile_triton.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/32185440/repro_time_text_embed_compile_triton.py)

title: [Inductor][AOTI][B200] TorchBench compilation latency regressed 57% since Aug 11
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

The compiler performance dashboard shows a sustained AOTInductor compilation-latency regression for TorchBench bfloat16 inference on B200:

| Date | Workflow / commit | Geomean compilation latency |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Aug 11 | [31468859815](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/31468859815) / `b2329090622d` | 19.76 s |
| Aug 12 | [31574146715](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/31574146715) / `1394bc6924ad` | 25.52 s (+29.1%) |
| Aug 13 | [31677954602](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/31677954602) / `04a7716a37e2` | 30.96 s (+21.3% day/day, +56.7% vs Aug 11) |

This is above the dashboard's 15% compilation-latency regression threshold on both days.

This is not caused by a changing model cohort: all three AOTInductor reports contain the same 43 models. Comparing Aug 11 to Aug 13, 21/43 models are more than 15% slower and the median model ratio is 1.147. Several models have much larger changes:

| Model | Aug 11 | Aug 13 | Ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `basic_gnn_edgecnn` | 7.00 s | 50.16 s | 7.17x |
| `shufflenet_v2_x1_0` | 13.51 s | 75.74 s | 5.61x |
| `mnasnet1_0` | 11.51 s | 51.87 s | 4.51x |
| `phlippe_densenet` | 12.88 s | 56.67 s | 4.40x |
| `functorch_dp_cifar10` | 10.45 s | 45.25 s | 4.33x |
| `densenet121` | 27.86 s | 110.09 s | 3.95x |

The spikes are not uniform: some models spiked on Aug 12 and recovered on Aug 13, while others first spiked on Aug 13. This may be B200 AOTI-specific resource contention or flakiness rather than a single deterministic code regression, but the aggregate has remained above the prior baseline for two consecutive runs.

Cross-checks make the signal look specific to B200 AOTInductor:

- AOTInductor TorchBench bfloat16 inference stayed stable over Aug 12 → Aug 13 on A100 (32.85 → 32.93 s), H100 (26.95 → 27.02 s), and MI355X (15.42 → 14.90 s).
- Other B200 compiler modes stayed stable over Aug 11 → Aug 12 → Aug 13: default (9.69 → 9.63 → 9.71 s), cudagraphs (7.97 → 7.89 → 7.84 s), and cpp_wrapper (13.55 → 13.50 → 13.59 s).
- The Aug 13 workflow as a whole failed because other jobs had runner/container infrastructure failures, but the [TorchBench benchmark job](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/actions/runs/31677954602/job/94382983210) succeeded and uploaded a complete 43-model AOTInductor report.

The first observed bad range is `b2329090622d..1394bc6924ad` (Aug 11 to Aug 12). A repeat on a clean B200 runner would help distinguish runner noise from a code regression before bisecting that range.

### Versions

PyTorch main, B200 CUDA benchmark runners, bfloat16 inference, TorchBench AOTInductor.

title: [inductor][cpu] Vectorized float64 `torch.acosh` returns `inf` for inputs above 1.34e154 under `torch.compile` (eager and the scalar tail are finite): `Vectorized<double>::acosh` squares its argument
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** `torch.acosh` on a float64 tensor of 1e200 returns `461.21` in eager and in the compiled function when the tensor has 3 elements, while the compiled function returns `inf` as soon as the tensor has 8 or more elements (torch 2.14.0 and nightly, Windows/MSVC and Linux/gcc); float32 is unaffected. A user sees the same element come out finite or infinite depending only on how long the tensor is, with no error. Because the vectorized C++ backend lowers `acosh` to `Vectorized<double>::acosh()`, which is SLEEF's `log(x + sqrt(x*x - 1))` and overflows in `x*x` above `sqrt(DBL_MAX) ≈ 1.34e154`, rather than the stable form `std::acosh` uses in the scalar tail and in the eager kernel, only the vector body of the loop is wrong.

```python
import torch

compiled = torch.compile(torch.acosh)
for n in (3, 8, 64):
    x = torch.full((n,), 1e200, dtype=torch.float64)
    print(f"n={n:2d}  eager {torch.acosh(x)[0].item():.6g}   compiled {compiled(x)[0].item():.6g}")
for v in (1.34e154, 1.35e154, 1e308):
    x = torch.full((16,), v, dtype=torch.float64)
    print(f"x={v:.3g}  eager {torch.acosh(x)[0].item():.6g}   compiled {compiled(x)[0].item():.6g}")
```

```
n= 3  eager 461.21   compiled 461.21
n= 8  eager 461.21   compiled inf
n=64  eager 461.21   compiled inf
x=1.34e+154  eager 355.584   compiled 355.584
x=1.35e+154  eager 355.591   compiled inf
x=1e+308  eager 709.889   compiled inf
```

**Root cause and possible fix.** `CppVecOverrides.acosh` in `torch/_inductor/codegen/cpp.py` emits `x.acosh()`, i.e. `Vectorized<double>::acosh()`, which calls `Sleef_acoshd*_u10`; SLEEF computes `log(x + sqrt((x - 1) * (x + 1)))` and the product overflows for `x > sqrt(DBL_MAX)`. The scalar backend emits `std::acosh(x)`, which handles the whole range. This is the float64 counterpart of the float32 `asinh` overflow fixed for the vector backend by using a stable formula (#152299); the same treatment works here: for large `|x|` use `log(x) + log(2)`, or in general `log1p((x - 1) + sqrt((x - 1) * (x + 1)))` computed with `x - 1` factored so nothing is squared.

### Error logs

No error is raised; the compiled result is `inf` where eager is finite, as shown above.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64
Python version: 3.14.7 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900T @ 1.50GHz (AVX2)
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.14.0+cpu
```

Same output on nightly 2.15.0.dev20260911+cpu and on Linux (gcc, torch 2.14.0+cpu and nightly 2.15.0.dev20260921+cpu). On a Tesla T4 the compiled CUDA result is finite and matches eager, so this is specific to the CPU vector backend.

title: [inductor][cpu] `torch.erfinv` loses accuracy near ±1 under `torch.compile`: relative error up to 7.5e-3 in float32 and 3.6e-3 in float64 where eager matches a 30-digit reference
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** `torch.erfinv` on CPU returns `3.8325069` in eager for float32 `x = 0.99999994` and `5.8635847` for float64 `x = 1 - 1e-16`, both matching a 30-digit reference, while the Inductor-compiled function returns `3.8035836` and `5.8426883` (relative error 7.5e-3 and 3.6e-3 with MSVC, 7.8e-6 and 6.2e-5 with glibc; torch 2.14.0 and nightly, scalar and vector paths). A user computing normal quantiles from probabilities close to 1 (`sqrt(2) * erfinv(2p - 1)`) gets tail values off in the third digit with no error, and the error grows smoothly toward ±1. Because the C++ backend emits `calc_erfinv` from `ATen/native/Math.h` (a rational guess plus two Newton steps whose correction `erf(x) - y` cancels near ±1) rather than the eager kernel's algorithm, every input with `|x| > 0.999` is affected, float64 included.

```python
import torch
from mpmath import mp, erfinv as mp_erfinv

mp.dps = 30
cases = ((torch.float32, [0.99, 0.9999, 0.999999, 0.9999999, 0.99999994]), (torch.float64, [0.999, 0.999999999, 1 - 1e-12, 1 - 1e-14, 1 - 1e-16]))
torch._dynamo.reset()
compiled = torch.compile(torch.erfinv)
for dtype, values in cases:
    for v in values:
        x = torch.full((16,), v, dtype=dtype)
        ref = float(mp_erfinv(mp.mpf(x[0].item())))
        e, c = torch.erfinv(x)[0].item(), compiled(x)[0].item()
        print(f"{str(dtype):14s} x={x[0].item()!r:22s} eager rel err {abs(e - ref) / ref:.1e}   compiled rel err {abs(c - ref) / ref:.1e}   (eager {e:.8g}, compiled {c:.8g}, reference {ref:.8g})")
```

```
torch.float32  x=0.9900000095367432     eager rel err 1.4e-08   compiled rel err 1.8e-07   (eager 1.8213866, compiled 1.8213869, reference 1.8213866)
torch.float32  x=0.9998999834060669     eager rel err 5.1e-09   compiled rel err 3.5e-07   (eager 2.7510355, compiled 2.7510364, reference 2.7510354)
torch.float32  x=0.9999989867210388     eager rel err 2.4e-08   compiled rel err 4.0e-06   (eager 3.4570746, compiled 3.4570887, reference 3.4570747)
torch.float32  x=0.9999998807907104     eager rel err 3.1e-08   compiled rel err 6.8e-06   (eager 3.7439213, compiled 3.7439468, reference 3.7439212)
torch.float32  x=0.9999999403953552     eager rel err 1.0e-08   compiled rel err 7.5e-03   (eager 3.8325069, compiled 3.8035836, reference 3.8325069)
torch.float64  x=0.999                  eager rel err 0.0e+00   compiled rel err 4.0e-15   (eager 2.3267538, compiled 2.3267538, reference 2.3267538)
torch.float64  x=0.999999999            eager rel err 0.0e+00   compiled rel err 1.0e-09   (eager 4.3200054, compiled 4.3200054, reference 4.3200054)
torch.float64  x=0.999999999999         eager rel err 0.0e+00   compiled rel err 5.5e-07   (eager 5.0420319, compiled 5.0420291, reference 5.0420319)
torch.float64  x=0.99999999999999       eager rel err 0.0e+00   compiled rel err 4.8e-05   (eager 5.4725525, compiled 5.4728131, reference 5.4725525)
torch.float64  x=0.9999999999999999     eager rel err 0.0e+00   compiled rel err 3.6e-03   (eager 5.8635847, compiled 5.8426883, reference 5.8635847)
```

The compiled result is the same for a 3-element tensor (scalar C++ path) and a 64-element one (vectorized path), so both code paths share the cause. `backend="aot_eager"` matches eager. On Linux (gcc, glibc) the same program gives smaller but still large errors — float32 `erfinv(0.99999994)` = `3.8325369` (relative error 7.8e-6 against 1.0e-8 for eager) and float64 `erfinv(1 - 1e-16)` = `5.8639485` (6.2e-5 against 0) — so the size of the error depends on the C library's `erf` and `exp`, while the loss of digits itself does not.

**Root cause and possible fix.** `torch/_inductor/codegen/cpp.py` lowers `erfinv` to `calc_erfinv(x)` in the scalar backend and to `x.erfinv()` in the vector backend, which is `Vectorized<T>::erfinv() = map(calc_erfinv)`. `calc_erfinv` in `ATen/native/Math.h` (Pavlis, 1996) forms a rational initial approximation and then applies two Newton steps `x -= (erf(x) - y) / (2/√π · exp(-x²))`; for `y` near ±1 the numerator `erf(x) - y` is the difference of two numbers that agree to almost all their digits, so the correction carries only a few significant digits and two steps do not converge. The eager CPU kernel reaches full precision on the same inputs, so the C++ backend should call the same routine the eager kernel uses, or compute the tail via `erfcinv` (`sqrt(-log(...))` on `1 - |y|`, which is exact for these inputs) with the Newton steps expressed through `erfc` instead of `erf`.

### Error logs

No error is raised; the compiled values differ from eager as shown above.

### Versions

```
PyTorch version: 2.14.0+cpu
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64
Python version: 3.14.7 (64-bit runtime)
Is CUDA available: False
CPU: 11th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-11900T @ 1.50GHz
[pip3] mpmath==1.3.0
[pip3] numpy==2.5.2
[pip3] torch==2.14.0+cpu
```

Same output on nightly 2.15.0.dev20260911+cpu. On Linux (gcc/glibc) the compiled errors are smaller but still far above eager's (see above). On a Tesla T4 (2.14.0+cu130 and nightly) the compiled CUDA kernel matches the reference, so this is specific to the CPU C++ backend.

title: [inductor] `avg_pool1d/2d` backward with `ceil_mode=True` divides the overhanging last window by the full kernel size, so the compiled gradient is wrong where eager and `aot_eager` agree; forward is correct
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** For `F.avg_pool1d` / `F.avg_pool2d` with `ceil_mode=True` and the default `count_include_pad=True`, eager and `backend="aot_eager"` give gradient `1/2` to the two elements of a last window covering two of its three positions, while Inductor gives `1/3` (torch 2.14.0 and nightly, CPU and CUDA, 1-D and 2-D). The forward output is identical in every backend, so a compiled training run gets wrong gradients on the last row and column of every `AvgPool2d(kernel, stride, ceil_mode=True)` layer with no error. Because the backward lowering `avg_pool2d_backward` uses `scale = kH * kW` whenever `count_include_pad` is set, rather than the window clipped to the padded input (`min(hstart + kH, H + pad) - hstart`) used by the eager kernel and the forward lowering, exactly the windows that `ceil_mode` lets overhang are divided by too much.

```python
import torch, torch.nn.functional as F

def grad_of(f, x, backend=None):
    x = x.detach().clone().requires_grad_()
    (f if backend is None else torch.compile(f, backend=backend))(x).sum().backward()
    return x.grad

x1 = torch.arange(6.0).reshape(1, 1, 6)          # avg_pool1d(k=3, s=2, ceil_mode=True): windows [0,1,2] [2,3,4] [4,5]
f1 = lambda x: F.avg_pool1d(x, 3, stride=2, ceil_mode=True)
x2 = torch.arange(36.0).reshape(1, 1, 6, 6)      # the GoogLeNet-style AvgPool2d(3, stride=2, ceil_mode=True)
f2 = lambda x: F.avg_pool2d(x, 3, stride=2, padding=1, ceil_mode=True)
for name, f, x in (("avg_pool1d k=3 s=2 ceil_mode", f1, x1), ("avg_pool2d k=3 s=2 p=1 ceil_mode", f2, x2)):
    torch._dynamo.reset()
    print(name, "| forward same:", torch.allclose(f(x), torch.compile(f)(x)))
    for backend in (None, "aot_eager", "inductor"):
        g = grad_of(f, x, backend)
        print(f"    {str(backend):10s} grad of last elements {[round(v, 4) for v in g.flatten()[-4:].tolist()]}")
```

```
avg_pool1d k=3 s=2 ceil_mode | forward same: True
    None       grad of last elements [0.6667, 0.3333, 0.8333, 0.5]
    aot_eager  grad of last elements [0.6667, 0.3333, 0.8333, 0.5]
    inductor   grad of last elements [0.6667, 0.3333, 0.6667, 0.3333]
avg_pool2d k=3 s=2 p=1 ceil_mode | forward same: True
    None       grad of last elements [0.2778, 0.5556, 0.2778, 0.6944]
    aot_eager  grad of last elements [0.2778, 0.5556, 0.2778, 0.6944]
    inductor   grad of last elements [0.2222, 0.4444, 0.2222, 0.4444]
```

In the 1-D case the last window `[4, 5]` has two elements, so eager's backward spreads `grad_output[2]` as `1/2` to each (element 4 gets `1/3 + 1/2 = 0.8333`, element 5 gets `0.5`); Inductor spreads it as `1/3`. With `count_include_pad=False` the compiled gradient is right (that branch computes the window size), and so is `ceil_mode=False` (no window overhangs). `avg_pool3d` goes through the fallback kernel and is right.

**Root cause and possible fix.** In `torch/_inductor/lowering.py::avg_pool2d_backward`:

```python
if divisor_override is not None:
    scale = divisor_override
elif count_include_pad or not had_padding:
    scale = kernel_size[0] * kernel_size[1]
else:
    scale = compute_pool_size_without_padding(ph, pw)
```

The eager kernel (`avg_pool2d_backward_out_frame`) computes `pool_size = (min(hstart + kH, H + padH) - hstart) * (min(wstart + kW, W + padW) - wstart)` for `count_include_pad=True`, i.e. it clips to the padded input before dividing; only the later clipping to `[0, H)` is skipped. The fix is to use that clipped size (the `hend` / `wend` values that `compute_pool_size_without_padding` computes before its final `ops.minimum(hend, height)`) as `scale` when `count_include_pad` is set and any `ceil_mode` overhang exists, matching what the forward lowering `_avg_poolnd` already does.

### Error logs

No error is raised; the compiled backward returns different gradient values, as shown above.

title: [inductor] `torch.any` on a uint8 tensor returns bool under `torch.compile` (eager and `torch.all` keep uint8), so downstream uint8 arithmetic silently changes
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** `torch.any(x)` and `x.any(dim)` on a uint8 tensor return uint8 in eager and under `backend="aot_eager"`, while the Inductor-compiled function returns bool (torch 2.14.0 and nightly, CPU and CUDA); `torch.all` on the same tensor keeps uint8 under every backend. A user sees the compiled result change dtype without any warning, and arithmetic on it changes value because the bool is promoted to int64 instead of wrapping in uint8 (`torch.any(x) * 200 + 100` is `44` in eager and `300` compiled). Because Inductor registers its own `reduce_any` lowering that casts to bool and returns the bool reduction rather than going through the `_refs.any` decomposition that restores uint8 (which `aten.all` still uses), only `any` loses the legacy uint8 result type.

```python
import torch

x = torch.tensor([[0, 3], [0, 0]], dtype=torch.uint8)
for name, f in {"torch.any(x)": lambda x: torch.any(x), "torch.all(x)": lambda x: torch.all(x), "x.any(0)": lambda x: x.any(0),
                "any(x) * 200 + 100": lambda x: torch.any(x) * 200 + 100}.items():
    e = f(x)
    row = [f"eager {e.tolist()} {e.dtype}"]
    for backend in ("aot_eager", "inductor"):
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        c = torch.compile(f, backend=backend)(x)
        row.append(f"{backend} {c.tolist()} {c.dtype}")
    print(f"{name:20s} " + " | ".join(row))
```

```
torch.any(x)         eager 1 torch.uint8 | aot_eager 1 torch.uint8 | inductor True torch.bool
torch.all(x)         eager 0 torch.uint8 | aot_eager 0 torch.uint8 | inductor 0 torch.uint8
x.any(0)             eager [0, 1] torch.uint8 | aot_eager [0, 1] torch.uint8 | inductor [False, True] torch.bool
any(x) * 200 + 100   eager 44 torch.uint8 | aot_eager 44 torch.uint8 | inductor 300 torch.int64
```

**Root cause and possible fix.** `torch/_refs/__init__.py` has both `any` and `all` convert the result back to uint8 when the input is uint8 ("Preserves uint8 -- probably a legacy mask thing"), and `aten.all` reaches Inductor through that decomposition. `aten.any` does not: `torch/_inductor/lowering.py` registers `reduce_any`, which does `x = to_dtype(x, torch.bool)` and returns `make_reduction("any")(x, ...)`, so the result is bool. Either drop the dedicated lowering and let `aten.any` decompose like `aten.all`, or make `reduce_any` cast the result back to uint8 when the input dtype is uint8, matching the eager kernel.

### Error logs

No error is raised; the compiled function returns `torch.bool` where eager returns `torch.uint8`, and the values of the dependent arithmetic differ as shown above (`44` vs `300`).

title: [inductor] `torch.clamp` with a Python bound outside the dtype's range wraps the bound: `clamp(int8_tensor, -1000, 1000)` returns `-24` for every element
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** `torch.clamp` on an integer tensor with Python-integer bounds that do not fit the tensor's dtype does not agree between eager and Inductor: for an int8 tensor, `clamp(x, -1000, 1000)` returns `x` unchanged in eager on nightly (and raises "value cannot be converted to type int8_t without overflow" in eager on 2.14.0), while Inductor returns `-24` for every element on both versions, and `clamp(x, max=300)` turns `127` into `44`. A user who clamps to a generous range that happens to exceed a narrow dtype gets a tensor of constants after compiling, with no error in either version. Because Inductor converts the bound to the tensor's dtype before comparing (`1000 -> int8 -24`, `300 -> 44`), every integer clamp whose bound is outside the dtype's range is affected.

```python
import torch

x = torch.tensor([-128, -3, 0, 5, 127], dtype=torch.int8)
for name, fn in (("clamp(x, -1000, 1000)", lambda t: torch.clamp(t, -1000, 1000)),
                 ("clamp(x, max=300)", lambda t: torch.clamp(t, max=300))):
    out = []
    for backend in (None, "aot_eager", "inductor"):
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        try:
            out.append(str((fn if backend is None else torch.compile(fn, backend=backend))(x.clone()).tolist()))
        except Exception as e:
            out.append("raises " + type(e).__name__)
    print(f"{name:22s} eager {out[0]} | aot_eager {out[1]} | inductor {out[2]}")
```

torch 2.14.0+cpu:

```
clamp(x, -1000, 1000)  eager raises RuntimeError | aot_eager raises RuntimeError | inductor [-24, -24, -24, -24, -24]
clamp(x, max=300)      eager raises RuntimeError | aot_eager raises RuntimeError | inductor [-128, -3, 0, 5, 44]
```

nightly 2.15.0.dev20260911+cpu:

```
clamp(x, -1000, 1000)  eager [-128, -3, 0, 5, 127] | aot_eager [-128, -3, 0, 5, 127] | inductor [-24, -24, -24, -24, -24]
clamp(x, max=300)      eager [-128, -3, 0, 5, 127] | aot_eager [-128, -3, 0, 5, 127] | inductor [-128, -3, 0, 5, 44]
```

`1000` as int8 is `-24` and `300` as int8 is `44`: the lower bound `-1000` wraps to `24`, the upper bound to `-24`, and `min(max(x, 24), -24)` is `-24` everywhere.

Eager's behaviour changed with #193169 (saturate out-of-range integer scalar `clamp` bounds, part of #107702); the Inductor lowering was not updated with it, which is the remaining inconsistency reported here.

**Possible fix.** In the Inductor lowering of `clamp` / `clamp_min` / `clamp_max`, when a bound is a Python scalar and the input dtype is integral, saturate the bound to `torch.iinfo(dtype)` before it is turned into a constant of the input dtype (a bound beyond the range then becomes a no-op, which is what eager does on nightly), instead of casting it with wrap-around.

### Error logs

No error is raised under Inductor; the values differ as shown above.

title: [dynamic shapes] With `capture_scalar_outputs=True`, the NaN check `v != v` on `v = loss.item()` is folded to `False` at trace time: a "skip this step if the loss is NaN" branch is never taken (all backends); `v - v` and `v * 0` fold to `0.0`
body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

**Summary.** With `torch._dynamo.config.capture_scalar_outputs = True`, `v = loss.item()` is an unbacked SymFloat and the self-comparison `v != v` is simplified to `False` while tracing, so for a NaN loss eager takes the `if v != v:` branch and the compiled function takes the other one on every backend (torch 2.14.0 and nightly). A training step that skips the update when the loss is NaN, written with the standard `x != x` idiom, applies the NaN update after compilation, with no error and no recompilation. Because the symbol is simplified as a finite real rather than as an IEEE float, `v != v` becomes false and `v - v` and `v * 0` become `0`, so every simplification that does not hold for NaN or infinity is affected, while `math.isnan(v)` stays correct.

```python
import math
import torch

torch._dynamo.config.capture_scalar_outputs = True

def step(loss, param):
    v = loss.item()
    if v != v:                      # standard NaN check: skip the update
        return param
    return param - 0.1 * v

def step_isnan(loss, param):
    v = loss.item()
    if math.isnan(v):
        return param
    return param - 0.1 * v

param, nan = torch.ones(2), torch.tensor(float("nan"))
for name, fn in (("v != v", step), ("math.isnan(v)", step_isnan)):
    print(f"{name:14s} eager {fn(nan, param).tolist()}", end="")
    for backend in ("eager", "aot_eager", "inductor"):
        torch._dynamo.reset()
        print(f"   {backend} {torch.compile(fn, backend=backend)(nan, param).tolist()}", end="")
    print()

sub = lambda t: t.item() - t.item()
torch._dynamo.reset()
print("v - v for v = inf:  eager", sub(torch.tensor(float("inf"))), "  inductor", torch.compile(sub)(torch.tensor(float("inf"))))
```

```
v != v         eager [1.0, 1.0]   eager [nan, nan]   aot_eager [nan, nan]   inductor [nan, nan]
math.isnan(v)  eager [1.0, 1.0]   eager [1.0, 1.0]   aot_eager [1.0, 1.0]   inductor [1.0, 1.0]
v - v for v = inf:  eager nan   inductor 0.0
```

Other forms from the same family (Inductor): `v != v` returned as a value is `False` for NaN, `v == v` is `True`, `torch.ones(2) * (v == v)` is `[1., 1.]` instead of `[0., 0.]`, `max(v, 0.0)` and `min(v, 0.0)` return `0.0` for NaN where Python returns `nan`, and `v * 0` is `0.0` for NaN and infinity.

**Possible fix.** The relational and arithmetic simplifications are valid for finite reals only. Options, from narrow to broad: special-case identical operands in `SymFloat.__eq__` / `__ne__` (and the `sym_node` handlers behind them) so that `v != v` is traced as `isnan(v)` rather than handed to SymPy; create unbacked float symbols without the `real=True` / finiteness assumptions so that `Ne(v, v)`, `v - v` and `0 * v` are not reduced; or, when a simplification of a float expression relies on finiteness, record a runtime assertion (`torch._check(math.isfinite(v))`) so that the NaN case fails loudly instead of taking the wrong branch.

### Error logs

No error, no graph break, no recompilation.

### Versions

```
OS: Microsoft Windows 11 Pro for Workstations (10.0.26200 64-bit)
MSVC: Microsoft (R) C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19.44.35228 for x64
```
